claims.text: A machine-learning–augmented free-energy scheme can replace costly explicit ab initio molecular dynamics for fusion and high-temperature thermodynamic predictions.
Sparse ab initio training samples can capture vibrational anharmonicity and electron–vibration coupling.
The proposed scheme can provide rapid and accurate predictions of fusion and high-temperature thermodynamic properties.
Elemental and binary systems near melting exhibit significant anharmonic and electron–vibration effects in their solid and liquid phases.
An active-learning framework can train high-fidelity interatomic potentials from a limited set of ab initio data covering both solid and liquid phases.
The trained potentials can predict phase free energies, including vibrational entropy, at reduced computational cost.
Iterative refinement with ab initio samples from critical solid and liquid regions can make the ML potential reproduce electron–vibration coupling and anharmonic vibrations.
Sufficient sampling of the relevant configurational space near the phase transition allows an ML potential to approximate ab initio free-energy differences accurately.
Combining the speed of ML potentials with targeted ab initio training data can preserve complex entropy contributions while substantially reducing computational cost.
The ML method is expected to produce free-energy estimates within a few percent of explicit ab initio free energies.
The ML method is expected to operate at approximately one-tenth the computational cost of explicit ab initio molecular-dynamics workflows.
The proposed method should scale better than TOR-TILD for high-entropy systems.
The method is primarily applicable to elemental and binary alloys within ±15% of their melting temperature.
Extension of the method to multicomponent high-entropy systems is not yet fully verified.
Multicomponent systems have a much larger configurational space, which may prevent ML potentials from capturing all relevant electron–vibration and anharmonic effects across both phases.
The hypothesis would be falsified if errors in phase free-energy differences, melting point, or latent heat exceed 5%–10% relative to ab initio benchmarks in elemental or binary systems.
The hypothesis would also be falsified if the method fails to reduce computational cost significantly relative to both TOR-TILD and explicit ab initio molecular dynamics.
